    MQ#

    jimble's MQ makes a DB table the queue. No separate middleware. The big thing you get is that it shares your transaction.

    Writing one#

    public class NoticeExecutor extends MqExecutor {

	@Override
	public String queueName () { return "mq_blog"; }

	@Override
	public String key () { return "notice"; }

	@Override
	public MqExecuteType executeType () { return MqExecuteType.short_time; }

	@Override
	public MqStatus execute (DB db, Data row) {

		Data data = row.getDataOptional("data");

		// ... do the work

		return MqStatus.completed;

	}

}
    • queueName() is the table name. One table per queue
    • key() is the kind. You can mix several kinds in one table
    • executeType() is short_time or long_time. It changes how messages are pulled off
    • Return anything other than MqStatus.completed and it runs again, up to maxRetry()

    Enqueueing#

    try (Tx tx = db.begin()) {

	long id;
	try {
		id = db.insertKey(
			SQL.insert(Post.instance())
				.value(Post.title, request.getString("title"))
				.value(Post.body, request.getString("body"))
				.value(Post.image_name, request.getStringOptional("image_name"))
				.value(Post.published, request.getBoolean("published"))
				.value(Post.created_at, new Date())
		);
	} catch (SqlExecuteException ex) {
		return -1;                   // tx.commit() まで来ないので、抜けたら巻き戻る
	}

	new NoticeExecutor().put(db, new Data()
		.putData("post_id", id)
		.putData("title", request.getString("title")));

	tx.commit();                     // 記事とキューを一緒に確定して終わる

	/*
	 * コミットしてから流す。
	 * 先に流すと、ロールバックしたときに
	 * 「入っていない記事のお知らせ」だけが届く。
	 */
	PostFeedHandler.notifyNewPost(request.getStringOptional("title"));

	return id;

}

    Call put() inside the transaction. It is the same DB, so rolling back throws away what you queued along with everything else. "The mail went out but the order was never created" cannot happen.

    You can also queue for a later time.

    new NoticeExecutor().put(db, data, scheduledAt);

    It will run twice#

    The same message can be executed twice. The process dying partway through the work is the usual reason.

    So write it so that running it again lands in the same place.

    • For mail, look at the sent record before you send
    • For a total, write the value in rather than adding to it
    • For an external API, attach an idempotency key

    "Exactly once" is not something a distributed system can give you. jimble does not pretend it can.

    Rows left running#

    If a process dies partway through, the row stays running. running rows older than mq.stale (10 minutes by default) are put back to waiting every mq.recover_interval (1 minute by default) (since 2.7.8; before that only when the queue started). Putting a row back counts as one retry, and a row that has used up maxRetry() becomes dead. Several servers doing this at once do not count twice.

    Careful

    Make mq.stale longer than your longest job. A job that runs longer than mq.stale is put back while it is still running, and another worker runs it again (it runs twice). When that happens, the old job that finishes later does not write its result (only a row still in the state it was claimed in is updated; since 2.7.8). If the log says the row "was claimed again while it was being processed", raise mq.stale.

    mq {
	stale            = 10m   # running rows older than this are treated as left behind by a dead process
	recover_interval = 1m    # how often to put them back; 0s means only when the queue starts
}

    Registering it and running it#

    // create the table
new MqQueue(NoticeExecutor.QUEUE_NAME).install();

// register the Executor (no classpath scanning)
MqRegistry.add(NoticeExecutor::new);

    Pulling messages off and running them is a batch's job. Write one batch — something like MqWorkerBatch — register it the same way as any other batch, and run it on cron.

    Only one poller per queue reads the DB. When workers are free, it takes as many messages as there are free workers with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and hands them straight to those workers (nothing is read ahead; up to 2.5.4 it took one message at a time). However many servers run the queue, each message is taken by exactly one worker (it can still be processed twice in the cases described above). mq.thread_count.<type> is how many messages are processed in parallel; raising it does not add connections borrowed while the queue is idle (up to 2.1.2 every worker polled the DB itself, so a slow DB filled one connection per worker at once).

    Choosing the data sources a queue lives on#

    With several data sources, a queue's table is created on every data source, and the poller visits them all in turn. A database that does not use queues (a shared one, say) can be left out (since 2.7.8).

    db {
	main   { main = true, ..., mq = false }   # no queues on this data source
	shop_a { url = "..." }
	shop_b { url = "..." }
}

mq.queues {
	mq_notice { data_sources = ["shop_a", "shop_b"] }   # where this queue lives (unset means every data source with mq = true)
}
    • A data source that is left out gets no table, and is not visited for claiming, for recovering stale rows (recoverStale), or for counting (pendingCount)
    • The poller orders the data sources by name and starts right after the one it last claimed from (since 2.7.8). One data source with a long backlog does not hold back the others (they are visited within "number of data sources" claims)
    • With both settings, the queue lives only on data sources that satisfy both. An unknown name in data_sources stops startup
    • put on a database of a data source that is left out throws MqException (nobody would process it)
    • Keep the queue table in the same database as the business tables, so enqueueing and the business update roll back together

    Note

    The scheduler's queue (scheduler.queue_name, mq_scheduler by default) lives on the main data source only (since 2.7.8). The scheduler's own tables (batch_master and the rest) and the admin screen's enqueueing are on the main data source, so the queue is created there and claimed from there regardless of db.<name>.mq. Rows put on other data sources are no longer claimed. To keep a queue of your own on the main data source only, use MqQueue.mainOnly("name") and return true from mainOnly() in the MqExecutor that puts to it.

    When one data source goes down#

    With several data sources, if one goes down (cannot connect, cannot read the table), the queue keeps running on the other data sources (since 2.7.9).

    • The poller retries the data source that is down after a pause (1 second, doubling up to 30 seconds) and skips it meanwhile, so waiting for a connection to an unreachable database does not hold back the other data sources' rows
    • A log line is written when it goes down, when a retry still fails, and when it comes back (not on every round)
    • Recovering stale rows (recoverStale) skips the data source that is down and recovers the others, so the queue starts even if one is down at startup
    • pendingCount() leaves out the data source that is down and returns the rest (it used to throw)
    • The poller does not stop on an unexpected failure either (it logs, waits a little and goes on)

    Visiting only the databases that have work#

    With dozens of data sources, the poller visits even the empty ones on every round. Whether the system is idle or only one database has work, SELECTs grow with the number of data sources. Set mq.hint and putting a message leaves a "this data source has work" hint; the poller then visits only the data sources with a hint (since 2.7.8).

    mq {
	hint           = redis   # off (default: visit everything every round) | memory | redis
	sweep_interval = 10s     # how often every data source is visited (rows without a hint are picked up within this)
}
    mq.hint Where hints live When it fits
    off (default) Nowhere; every round visits everything (as before) Few data sources
    memory Inside the same process only Putting and claiming happen in the same process
    redis Inside the process and in a Redis set Put from the web, claim in a batch process (different processes)

    With hints, the poller visits only:

    • data sources with a hint (kept for 5 seconds after the hint is seen, so a putting transaction that has not committed yet is not missed)
    • data sources that last returned as many rows as were wanted (there may be more)
    • every data source, once per sweep_interval

    A hint only makes the poller look sooner; nothing is lost without it. If Redis is down, neither putting nor claiming fails (a log line is written) and the rows are picked up by the full round.

    Careful

    A row without a hint can wait up to sweep_interval. Rows get no hint when another process put them with a time (scheduled_at), when another process put them under memory, or while Redis was down. Retries are not delayed: the poller's own process keeps a hint for the retry time.

    Claiming SELECTs measured on a local MySQL with one queue, two workers, poll_max = 1s and sweep_interval = 10s:

    Data sources Idle (off → redis) To the other databases while one gets 10 messages a second (off → redis)
    10 20/s → 2/s 837/s → 1.8/s
    30 54/s → 6/s 1,701/s → 5.8/s
